drills.q: Why is computing the full softmax infeasible for training Word2Vec at vocabulary scale?
drills.a: The denominator sums exp(v'_w · v_wI) over every word in the vocabulary for every single training example -- O(V) dot products per example, infeasible for a 100k+ word vocabulary trained on billions of tokens.

drills.q: What's the practical training difference between Word2Vec and GloVe?
drills.a: Word2Vec is online/streaming, processing local context windows incrementally with no global matrix. GloVe is batch: it first builds the full word-word co-occurrence matrix, then factorizes it, requiring a full corpus pass before training starts.

drills.q: Derive the negative sampling objective from the full softmax skip-gram objective, and explain what each term does.
drills.a: Full softmax: p(wO|wI) = exp(v'_wO·v_wI) / Σ_w exp(v'_w·v_wI). Negative sampling reframes as binary classification: log σ(v'_wO·v_wI) + Σ_{i=1}^k E[log σ(−v'_wi·v_wI)]. The first term pushes the real pair's dot product up; the sum pushes k randomly sampled fake pairs' dot products down, turning O(V) into O(k) per example.

drills.q: Explain the theoretical connection between skip-gram with negative sampling and GloVe.
drills.a: Levy & Goldberg (2014) proved SGNS implicitly factorizes a word-context PMI matrix shifted by −log(k): v_wI·v'_wO ≈ PMI(wI,wO) − log(k). GloVe explicitly factorizes global co-occurrence counts via weighted least squares. They're not unrelated algorithms -- one performs implicit factorization via gradient descent on local prediction, the other explicit factorization of global counts.

drills.q: A team wants to embed product listings with heavy typos and brand-name variants. Word2Vec or fastText, and why?
drills.a: fastText -- it represents each word as a sum of character n-gram vectors (n=3-6), so morphologically related words and even unseen (misspelled/novel) words get a usable vector composed from known n-grams. Word2Vec/GloVe assign one opaque vector per whole word and have no representation at all for unseen tokens.

drills.q: Why can't a static embedding represent polysemy, and what architectural change fixed it?
drills.a: Static training assigns exactly one vector per word type by aggregating every training context into a single fixed point -- there's no mechanism to condition on the current sentence at inference time. ELMo (BiLSTM hidden states per token) then BERT (transformer + MLM) compute a different vector per token occurrence as a function of surrounding context, fixing this structurally rather than with more data.

drills.q: Design a query-autocomplete feature at high QPS with a sub-10ms latency budget. Static or contextual embeddings, and why?
drills.a: Static, almost certainly -- autocomplete needs sub-10ms responses at very high QPS, and its semantic needs (broad topical/lexical similarity) rarely depend on fine-grained context disambiguation. A precomputed static embedding index with ANN search meets the latency bar; a contextual forward pass per keystroke does not at reasonable infra cost.

drills.q: A team averages word embeddings to build document vectors for search and results are poor. Diagnose and fix.
drills.a: Mean-pooling destroys word order and negation, and is disproportionately influenced by the most frequent (least discriminative) words in the document -- the same failure raw TF without IDF has. Weight the average by TF-IDF (SIF weighting) as a partial fix, but for genuine sentence-level semantics move to a model trained for that objective (Sentence-BERT-style) rather than patching averaging further.

drills.q: Nearest-neighbor search quality degrades after a routine embedding retraining. What are the two distinct failure modes to check?
drills.a: Quality degradation (the new embeddings are genuinely worse -- check against a held-out similarity/analogy or task-specific eval) versus alignment breakage (old and new vectors got mixed in the same index despite embedding spaces from separate training runs having arbitrary, incomparable orientation). The fix for the second is never serving a mixed index -- reindex fully after retraining.

drills.q: Design an embedding strategy for a platform needing both millions-of-documents batch content tagging and low-QPS quality-critical real-time search.
drills.a: These sit at different points on the latency/cost/accuracy curve. Batch tagging is throughput-bound not latency-bound, so it can afford contextual embeddings run offline for accuracy, or a lighter fastText/static pipeline if that's sufficient -- measure both. Real-time search is low-QPS but quality-critical: use a contextual embedding per query (cheap, one per search) against precomputed document embeddings (computed once offline) -- the standard asymmetric bi-encoder retrieve pattern.
